why_how.text: Texas sets out who must carry a Texas license so newcomers, nonresidents and service members each know which rule applies to them.
The learner license lets a new driver practice safely because an experienced, sober adult rides along.

scenario.text: Leah moves to Texas from another state and plans to keep driving on her old license for six months.

reasoning.text: New residents have a ninety-day clock to qualify for a Texas license, so six months is too long.

result.text: Leah applies for her Texas license within ninety days of moving in.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any licensed driver of any age can ride along as a learner's companion.

correction.text: The companion must be sober, watchful, at least twenty-one, and have at least a year of driving experience.

memory_support.text: Ninety days to switch, twenty-one to coach.

prompt.text: A friend who moved to Texas last month asks how long she has to qualify for a Texas license. What do you tell her?

answer.text: Ninety days from becoming a resident.

rationale.text: New residents get a ninety-day clock; only service members keep a Texas card through duty plus ninety days after.

lines.text: Who must hold a Texas license.

narration.text: Welcome to the first lesson on your Texas license. Before you learn any rule of the road, the handbook answers a basic question: who needs a Texas license at all, and how does a brand new driver start? This lesson covers residents and new residents, nonresidents who drive here on a home license, and military drivers. Then it moves to the learner license, the companion who must ride with you, what the learner card costs, and the school form that under-eighteen applicants must bring. By the end you will know which rule applies to you.

lines.text: Nonresidents may use home licenses in limits.

narration.text: Texas licenses cover residents, and a new resident has ninety days to qualify for one. Nonresidents can drive here on a home license within limits: those sixteen or older for Class C or M vehicles, and those eighteen or older for other classes when their home state offers reciprocity. Military drivers on home licenses are covered too, and a Texas card a service member already holds stays valid through service plus ninety days. So the question to ask is simple: am I a resident, a nonresident visitor, or a service member? Each group has its own rule.

lines.text: A sober, watchful companion rides along.
At least one year of experience.

narration.text: A learner license lets you practice, but never alone. Your companion must be sober and watchful, at least twenty-one years old, and have at least a year of driving experience. Applicants for the learner license run from fifteen to eighteen and must have passed the classroom part of driver education and their exams. The card costs sixteen dollars total and lasts until you turn eighteen. A practicing adult pays thirty-three dollars total for eight restricted years. Before a new card is issued, every earlier card you hold must be surrendered.

lines.text: Fresh for thirty days in session.
Fresh for ninety days over summer.

narration.text: If you are under eighteen and applying for the first time, you bring a Verification of Enrollment, or VOE, from your school. It proves you have a diploma, attended eighty days in the prior term, or attended forty-five days of a high school equivalency preparation program. The form has a shelf life. One issued while school is in session stays fresh for thirty days, while one issued during summer stays fresh for ninety days. Plan your trip to the driver license office so the form is still fresh when you arrive, or you will need a new one from your school.

lines.text: New resident: ninety days to qualify.
Service member: duty plus ninety days.

narration.text: Here is a trap built from similar numbers. Ninety days shows up more than once in this lesson, and each time it means something different. A new resident has ninety days to qualify for a Texas license. A service member's existing Texas card stays valid through duty plus ninety days after service ends. A school VOE issued over summer stays fresh for ninety days, but one issued during the school year lasts only thirty. When a practice question mentions ninety days, first ask who the person is, a newcomer, a service member, or a student, and then pick the matching rule.

lines.text: A friend moved here last month.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a friend moved to Texas last month and still drives on her old license. She asks how long she has to qualify for a Texas license. Work out your answer before reading on. The answer is ninety days from becoming a resident. She should not confuse that with the service member rule, which keeps an existing Texas card valid through duty plus ninety days after service. If she has a teen in the family applying for a learner license, that teen also needs a fresh school VOE and a sober companion at least twenty-one with a year of experience.

lines.text: Learners ride with an experienced adult.
Bring a fresh VOE if under eighteen.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. Residents need a Texas license, and new residents have ninety days to qualify. Some nonresidents and military drivers may drive here on a home license within the limits the handbook sets. A learner drives only with a sober, watchful companion at least twenty-one who has a year of experience. The learner card costs sixteen dollars total until eighteen, while a practicing adult pays thirty-three dollars total for eight restricted years. Under-eighteen first-timers bring a school VOE that is still fresh. Next comes hardship licensing and the graduated phases.

why_how.text: Graduated licensing gives new teen drivers experience in steps, with limits that ease as they prove themselves.
Hardship licenses exist for a few real needs, so approval depends on proof rather than convenience.

scenario.text: Sam is seventeen, holds a Phase Two license, and wants to drive three friends home from a movie at one in the morning.

reasoning.text: Phase Two allows only one young non-family passenger and bans midnight-to-five driving except for work, school, or emergency.

result.text: Sam may take only one friend, and a late movie is not an allowed reason to drive after midnight.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing a teen can get a hardship license just because driving would be convenient.

correction.text: Hardship approval is only for a money crisis, a family emergency, a vocational need, or a court order.

prompt.text: A seventeen-year-old in Phase Two wants to drive two young friends to a late party. Which limits does that break?

answer.text: Both: only one young non-family passenger is allowed, and a party is not a reason to drive between midnight and five.

rationale.text: Phase Two sets two separate limits, a passenger cap of one and a midnight-to-five ban outside work, school, or emergency.

narration.text: This lesson is about how teens move from a learner license toward full driving. Texas uses a graduated system, which means new drivers earn freedom in stages instead of all at once. There is also a hardship license for a small set of real needs. We will look at who can get a hardship license and why, how long the first phase lasts, the limits that apply in Phase Two, and the words printed on young drivers' cards. Each piece fits together, and the practice questions often mix them, so keep each limit tied to its own phase as you go.

A hardship license is for fifteen to eighteen year olds with a real need. An adult petitions in person, the teen completes full driver education and the exams, and approval comes only for a money crisis, a family emergency, a vocational need, or a court order. Everyone new to driving also goes through the graduated system, which requires the driving exam. Phase One means holding a learner license for at least six months, and a suspension stretches that time. Class M is different, because there is no Phase One wait before a motorcycle license.

Phase Two adds limits once you have your provisional license. You may carry only one young passenger who is not a family member. You may not drive between midnight and five in the morning unless it is for work, school, or an emergency. Drivers under eighteen may not use a wireless device except in an emergency. Cards for drivers sixteen to eighteen say PROVISIONAL, and cards issued before age twenty-one say UNDER twenty-one. Out-of-state teens are placed in Phase One or Phase Two based on the credential they already hold, and adult licenses run eight years.

lines.text: PROVISIONAL: holders aged sixteen to eighteen.
UNDER twenty-one: every card before twenty-one.
A teen card can show both.

narration.text: Here is a trap many learners fall into. Two markings sound alike but answer different questions. PROVISIONAL marks a license held by a driver from sixteen to eighteen who is still in the graduated system. UNDER twenty-one marks every card issued to someone younger than twenty-one, so it reaches further than PROVISIONAL does. A nineteen-year-old's card says UNDER twenty-one but is no longer provisional. When a question asks about the PROVISIONAL marking, think of the teen phases. When it asks about UNDER twenty-one, think of age alone, wherever the driver is in the system.

Here is a quick check: a seventeen-year-old in Phase Two wants to drive two young friends to a party that ends after midnight. Which rules does that break? Work it out before reading on. It breaks both Phase Two limits. Only one young non-family passenger may ride along, and a party is not one of the reasons to drive between midnight and five in the morning. The allowed reasons are work, school, or an emergency. Notice that the two limits are separate. Even with only one friend aboard, the late drive home would still break the midnight rule.

lines.text: Phase One lasts six learner months.
Phase Two: one rider, no midnight.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. A hardship license is for fifteen to eighteen year olds with a proven need, a money crisis, a family emergency, a vocational need, or a court order. The graduated system starts with at least six months on a learner license, and a suspension stretches that time. Phase Two allows one young non-family passenger, bans driving from midnight to five except for work, school, or an emergency, and bans wireless use under eighteen. Teen cards say PROVISIONAL, and all cards before twenty-one say UNDER twenty-one. Next we look at license classes.

why_how.text: License classes match the license to the vehicle, because heavier vehicles and combinations need more skill.
Knowing the class tells you which test and which fee apply.

scenario.text: Jordan, a sixteen-year-old who finished driver education, wants a license to drive the family car.

reasoning.text: A family car is a Class C vehicle, and the price path for a sixteen-year-old with education is sixteen dollars total.

result.text: Jordan applies for Class C on the education path, paying sixteen dollars total.

claim.text: Common mistake: assuming a Class C license also lets you ride a motorcycle.

correction.text: Class C never covers motorcycles; a motorcycle needs Class M after a passed state motorcycle course.

memory_support.text: A for combinations, B for heavy singles, C for cars.

prompt.text: A neighbor wants to add motorcycle privileges to her current license. What does appending Class M cost?

rationale.text: Appending M to a live license costs sixteen dollars total, while renewing M later adds twelve dollars total.

narration.text: This lesson sorts out the license classes. Texas uses letters to match the license to the vehicle you plan to drive. Class A and Class B cover heavier vehicles and combinations. Class C covers the everyday vehicles most new drivers use. Class M covers motorcycles and has its own course requirement. Along the way you will learn what each class costs on different paths. Questions on this topic usually describe a vehicle or a driver and ask which class fits, so focus on what defines each class rather than memorizing every number at once.

Class A covers everything in Classes B and C plus heavy combinations, where the towed vehicle weighs more than ten thousand pounds. Class B covers everything in Class C plus heavy single vehicles, which may tow ten thousand pounds or a farm trailer up to twenty thousand pounds. Neither class covers motorcycles. For an adult, each costs thirty-three dollars total for eight years, and drivers through age twenty-four need education. A seventeen-year-old with education pays sixteen dollars total. The key difference is combination weight for Class A and single-vehicle weight for Class B.

title.text: Class C and the M course

lines.text: Class C: lighter vehicles, small trailers.
Class M needs a state course.

narration.text: Class C covers lighter vehicles, small trailers, and certified three-wheel autocycles, but never motorcycles. It costs thirty-three dollars total for an adult, sixteen dollars total at sixteen with driver education, or six dollars total at fifteen on the hardship path. A Class M license first requires a passed state-approved motorcycle course. Applicants under eighteen also show classroom driver education and either a learner license or a valid Class C license. So a car license and a motorcycle license are separate steps, and the course is required for the motorcycle license.

lines.text: Append fee differs from renewal fee.

narration.text: Motorcycle licensing opens at sixteen after the required course hours, or at fifteen for small bikes through hardship or courses. An adult Class M costs thirty-three dollars total and a young applicant pays sixteen dollars total. Adding M to a license you already hold costs sixteen dollars total, and when you renew a license with M, you pay twelve dollars total on top of the renewal fee. Disabled veterans rated sixty percent or more can skip these fees, except for commercial licenses and certain registrant cases. Keep the append fee and the renewal add-on separate.

lines.text: Class A: combined weight, heavy tow.

narration.text: Here is a trap built from two similar classes. Both Class A and Class B cover heavy vehicles, so learners mix them up. The difference is what gets weighed. Class A is about combinations, a vehicle towing another, judged by combined weight with a towed vehicle over ten thousand pounds. Class B is about a heavy single vehicle, judged by that vehicle's own weight, with lighter towing caps. If a question describes a truck pulling a heavy trailer, think Class A. If it describes one heavy truck with only a light trailer or none, think Class B.

Here is a quick check: a neighbor already holds a Class C license and wants to add motorcycle privileges. What does appending Class M to her live license cost? Work out your answer before reading on. It costs sixteen dollars total. Do not confuse that with the twelve dollars total that renewing M adds on top of a renewal later. Remember too that before she can get Class M at all, she must pass a state-approved motorcycle course, because a Class C license never covers motorcycles, even a small one, on its own. The course comes first, then the license.

lines.text: Class B heavy singles; Class C lighter vehicles.
Class M: motorcycles after a course.

narration.text: To wrap up, Class A covers heavy combinations plus Class B and C vehicles. Class B covers heavy single vehicles plus Class C vehicles. Class C covers lighter vehicles, small trailers and certified autocycles, but never motorcycles. Class C costs thirty-three dollars total as an adult, sixteen dollars total at sixteen with education, or six dollars total at fifteen on the hardship path. Class M opens at sixteen after a state motorcycle course, appending it costs sixteen dollars total, and renewing it adds twelve dollars total. Next we look at ID cards and what applicants must prove.

why_how.text: Every applicant proves who they are and that their vehicles are insured, so the state can trust the license it issues.
Finishing Impact Texas Drivers before exams makes sure every new driver hears the same safety lessons first.

scenario.text: Ana is applying for her first Texas license and owns a car.

reasoning.text: She must prove identity, Social Security, fitness and lawful presence, insure her car to Texas minimums, and finish Impact Texas Drivers.

result.text: Ana brings her proofs and insurance, completes Impact Texas Drivers, pays the fee, and then takes her exams.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the contribution checkboxes on the application are what make you an organ donor.

correction.text: The donor heart on the card front is the binding consent; the checkboxes are optional donations.

prompt.text: A cousin sees a heart and the word donor on his new card. What does that mean?

answer.text: It is conclusive consent to be an organ donor.

rationale.text: The donor heart is binding consent, while the contribution checkboxes are only optional donations.

narration.text: This lesson covers the paperwork side of getting licensed. First, Texas ID cards, which are not driver licenses but are issued by the same office. Then the choices you make on the application, including organ donation and optional contributions. Finally, the proofs every applicant must bring and the steps that must be finished before you take any exam. None of this is about driving skill, but it decides whether you can sit the exam at all, and the practice questions do ask about it, so give it the same care as the driving rules.

A Texas ID card can be issued at any age. Cards for people under twenty-one are printed in a vertical layout. An ID card costs sixteen dollars total for six years through age fifty-nine, or six dollars total after that. The back of the card allows two emergency contacts, and you may handwrite allergy drugs there, because DPS prints no medical facts on the card. That last point matters: if a question asks whether the state prints your medical conditions on the card, the answer is no. Any medical note you want carried is something you add yourself.

Your card can show a heart with the word donor, and that is conclusive consent to donate. Separately, applicants may choose to fund causes such as blindness care, Donate Life, veterans, evidence testing, or youth fees. You file in person, and voter registration is offered from seventeen years and ten months. Men eighteen to twenty-five are registered with selective service automatically. Every applicant proves identity, Social Security, fingerprints, medical fitness and lawful presence, and surrenders any foreign license. Your exams, convictions and crashes stay on your permanent record.

Here is a trap that catches careful readers. The application offers two kinds of giving, and they are easy to blur together. The donor heart printed on the front of your card is binding consent to donate organs. It is the decision itself. The contribution checkboxes are something else, optional donations of money to causes such as Donate Life or veterans programs. Checking a box does not make you an organ donor, and choosing to be a donor does not cost you anything. When a question asks what the heart means, answer consent; when it asks about the boxes, answer optional donations.

lines.text: A heart on a new card.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a cousin picks up his new card and sees a heart with the word donor on the front. What does that marking mean? Work out your answer before reading on. It means conclusive consent to be an organ donor. It is not a record of a money contribution, because those are separate optional checkboxes on the application. Before he got that card, he also had to prove his identity, Social Security, fingerprints, fitness and lawful presence, and insure any vehicle he owns to Texas minimums, or swear that none qualifies.

Let us sum up. ID cards issue at any age, are vertical under twenty-one, and carry up to two emergency contacts on the back, with no printed medical facts. A donor heart is binding consent, while contribution checkboxes are optional. Applicants prove identity, Social Security, prints, fitness and lawful presence, and insure each owned vehicle to Texas minimums. New residents register their vehicles, fees come before exams, drivers under twenty-five finish driver education, and everyone finishes Impact Texas Drivers before the exam. Under-eighteen filings need a guardian signature. Next come the exams themselves.

why_how.text: Exams check that you know the rules and can drive safely before Texas trusts you alone on the road.
Knowing what the examiner grades helps you practice the right skills.

scenario.text: Chris fails the knowledge exam on the first try.

reasoning.text: A failed exam parks the application for ninety days, during which Chris can try again.

result.text: Chris studies, passes within the ninety days, and receives a forty-five-day temporary card after the driving exam.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking each license class has its own, different passing score on the knowledge exam.

correction.text: Class C, Class M, and Class A and B knowledge exams all pass at seventy percent or better.

memory_support.text: Seventy to pass, thirty points to lose.

prompt.text: Your sister fails her knowledge exam this morning. What happens to her application?

answer.text: It is parked for ninety days.

rationale.text: A failed exam parks the application ninety days, while passing earns a forty-five-day temporary card.

narration.text: This lesson walks through the exams. You will see what happens when you fail and when you pass, what score passes a knowledge exam, who must take the driving exam, what the driving exam costs in some cases, what makes you fail it, and what the examiner watches. Understanding the process helps you plan, and it also takes some of the stress out of exam day, because you will know what to expect from the moment you arrive to the moment you leave with a temporary card. Hold on to the outcomes, the passing mark, and the graded skills.

lines.text: Failure parks the application ninety days.

narration.text: If you fail an exam, your application is parked for ninety days while you prepare to try again. Adults who already hold a valid license may be able to skip exams. When you pass, you earn a forty-five-day temporary card. Knowledge exams cover Class C original licenses, Class M, where the exam can be waived, and Class A and B rules, and all of them pass at seventy percent or better. A vision check is part of the process too, and it may require you to wear corrective lenses or see a doctor before you can be licensed. Plan for both checks on exam day.

The driving exam comes after you pass your other exams and prove insurance, and you take it in a vehicle that matches your license class. No one under eighteen is excused from it. It is given at driver license offices and at approved schools, and learners do not take it with a learner license. Stepping up a class or removing restrictions costs ten dollars, and appending Class M costs fifteen dollars. You fail if you break a traffic law, disobey the examiner, drive dangerously, or lose more than thirty points. The point limit is the key number to keep.

The examiner grades a long list of skills: vehicle control, observation, positioning, signaling, parking, quick stops, backing, obeying signs and signals, using the clutch where there is one, intersections, turns, right of way, following distance, passing, lane use, and posture. You may use your cameras, but automated parking features are not allowed during the exam. So practice the basics until they feel natural, especially looking around before every move, keeping a steady position in your lane, and signaling every turn and lane change in good time.

Here is a trap built from two exam clocks. Both outcomes come with a number of days, and learners often swap them. A failed exam parks your application for ninety days. That is the window for trying again. A passed exam earns a forty-five-day temporary card, which you carry while your permanent card is made. So ninety goes with failure and waiting, and forty-five goes with success and the temporary card. If a practice question asks what you receive after passing, the answer is the forty-five-day card, not a ninety-day anything.

Here is a quick check: your sister fails her knowledge exam this morning. What happens to her application? Work out your answer before reading on. Her application is parked for ninety days while she prepares to try again. If she had passed, she would have moved on and, after the driving exam, received a forty-five-day temporary card. Remember the passing mark too. Her knowledge exam, like every class of knowledge exam in Texas, passes at seventy percent or better, so she needs at least that score on her next try. A steady review plan makes that easier.

To wrap up, failing an exam parks your application for ninety days, and passing earns a forty-five-day temporary card. Every knowledge exam, whether Class C, Class M, or Class A and B, passes at seventy percent or better. The driving exam follows passed exams and proven insurance, uses a vehicle that matches your class, and excuses no one under eighteen. Upgrading costs ten dollars and appending M costs fifteen. You fail for breaking the law, disobeying the examiner, driving dangerously, or losing more than thirty points. Next we cover carrying and renewing your license.

why_how.text: Carrying your license lets officers and other drivers in a crash confirm who you are.
Reporting changes and renewing on time keeps your record accurate and your license valid.

scenario.text: Pat moves across town and wonders whether to wait for the renewal notice.

reasoning.text: An address move must be reported within thirty days, and renewal notices are only a courtesy.

result.text: Pat reports the move within thirty days and does not rely on a renewal notice.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking that renewing every eight years means you never have to visit an office.

correction.text: Licenses renew every eight years, but every driver must still appear in person at least every sixteen years for vision and biometrics.

memory_support.text: Renew at eight, appear at sixteen.

prompt.text: A coworker caught driving unlicensed for the first time asks about the fine. What is it?

rationale.text: A first unlicensed offense brings a two hundred dollar fine; a second within a year falls in a twenty-five to two hundred dollar band, and deadly uninsured crashes bring jail.

lines.text: Carry it and keep it valid.

narration.text: Getting a license is only the start. This lesson covers what you do with it afterward. You will learn who can ask to see your license, the penalties for driving without one, how to replace a lost card or report a move, and how renewal works, including when you must appear in person and who may not renew remotely. These rules matter because a license that is out of date or missing can bring fines even when you drive perfectly. Keep an eye on the deadlines and on the difference between the renewal cycle and the visit cycle.

lines.text: Carry it for officers and crashes.

narration.text: If you fail an exam, you reschedule. Once you pass, you carry your license and show it to officers and to the other people involved in a crash. Driving unlicensed brings a fine of two hundred dollars for a first offense, and a second offense within a year falls in a band from twenty-five to two hundred dollars. An unlicensed driver who causes a deadly crash without insurance faces Class A jail time. If you need to change a restriction on your license, you can do it at any driver license office, so there is no reason to drive under the wrong terms.

lines.text: Report a move within thirty days.

narration.text: A duplicate license or an address change costs eleven dollars total, and you must report a move within thirty days. Mail service costs ten dollars, and other changes are made in person. Special licenses have no remote service, and renewal notices are only a courtesy, so do not wait for one. Licenses renew every eight years, but you must visit an office at least every sixteen years for vision and biometrics. Some drivers cannot renew remotely, and service families can renew without exams within ninety days of discharge, while Texans out of state can mail in their fees and vision results.

Here is a trap built from two cycles. Both involve renewal, and both are multiples of eight, so they are easy to swap. Your license renews every eight years. That is the renewal cycle. Separately, every driver must appear in person at least every sixteen years for a vision check and biometrics such as a photo and fingerprints. In between, eligible drivers may renew remotely. So if a question asks how long a license lasts, think eight years. If it asks how often you must show up in person, think sixteen years. Remote renewal never removes the in-person visit.

Here is a quick check: a coworker is caught driving without a license for the first time and asks what the fine is. Work out your answer before reading on. The first offense brings a two hundred dollar fine. A second offense within a year falls in a band from twenty-five to two hundred dollars, and an unlicensed driver who causes a deadly crash without insurance faces Class A jail time. Remind your coworker that a license must be carried and shown to officers and to the other people involved in any crash, so it should be in hand every time.

lines.text: Renew at eight, appear at sixteen.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. Carry your license and show it to officers and to others in a crash. Driving unlicensed brings a two hundred dollar fine first, a twenty-five to two hundred dollar band on a second within a year, and Class A jail for deadly uninsured crashes. Duplicates and address changes cost eleven dollars total, and a move must be reported within thirty days, because renewal notices are only a courtesy. Licenses renew every eight years, and you appear in person at least every sixteen years for vision and biometrics. Next we turn to suspension and revocation.

why_how.text: Suspension and revocation protect everyone by removing drivers who break serious laws or repeat dangerous behavior.
Knowing the triggers helps you avoid the steps that lead to losing your license.

scenario.text: Taylor has collected four traffic convictions over the last twelve months.

reasoning.text: Four convictions in twelve months is a bad pattern that can lead to a hearing suspension.

result.text: Taylor's license may be suspended after a hearing, and reinstatement would then cost a fee.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a driver under twenty-one is only revoked for alcohol at point zero eight, like adults.

correction.text: Under twenty-one, any detectable alcohol brings revocation; point zero eight is the adult line.

memory_support.text: Adults point zero eight, minors none.

prompt.text: How many convictions in twenty-four months can lead to a hearing suspension?

rationale.text: Hearing review follows four convictions in twelve months or seven in twenty-four months.

narration.text: This lesson explains how a license can be taken away. Some suspensions are automatic and follow a conviction with no hearing at all. Others follow a hearing about a pattern of convictions or failures. Revocation is a more serious action, and intoxication is a common cause, with a different alcohol line for adults and for drivers under twenty-one. Courts can also order action on a license for reasons such as child support. You will also learn what it costs to get a license back. Keep each trigger tied to the right kind of action as you learn them.

Getting a license back after a suspension costs one hundred dollars, and after a revocation it costs one hundred twenty-five dollars, and you may also need SR-twenty-two proof of insurance. Intoxicated driving, drug, and assault convictions can open a revocation. Some acts suspend a license automatically, including failing to give aid in a crash, a deadly crash, felonies, repeat school bus violations, boating while intoxicated, evading arrest, driving while invalid, card fraud, graffiti, fake plates, false records, and racing. Automatic means no hearing comes first.

A hearing can lead to suspension when a driver shows a bad pattern, four convictions in twelve months or seven in twenty-four months, and also for exam and probation failures. Drivers under twenty-one are suspended automatically for alcohol, tobacco-class, drug, and certain other listed offenses. Minors can also face hearing suspensions for court orders, fines, repeat tickets, or delinquency. Intoxication revocation strikes adults at point zero eight, anyone who refuses a test, and any driver under twenty-one with detectable alcohol. Getting a revoked license back costs one hundred twenty-five dollars.

lines.text: Cancellation follows lies or lost approval.

narration.text: A license can also be cancelled, for example after an action in another state, a lost approval, a gap in the requirements, or a lie on the application. Separately, courts can order action on your license. The handbook lists child support, an ignition interlock order, overpayments, incapacity, dependency, and a lapsed annual renewal as reasons. Court-ordered actions are not a choice the department makes on its own; the order compels it. So when a question mentions unpaid child support and a license, think of a court order compelling action rather than an automatic traffic suspension.

title.text: Four in twelve, seven in twenty-four

lines.text: Either pattern can bring a hearing.

narration.text: Here is a trap built from two patterns. Both lead to a hearing, and the numbers are easy to mix up. Four convictions within twelve months is one bad pattern. Seven convictions within twenty-four months is the other. Notice that the longer window needs more convictions, not fewer. A driver with five convictions over two years has not reached either pattern yet, while a driver with four in a single year has. When a practice question gives a number of convictions, check the time window first, and then compare the count against the matching threshold.

Here is a quick check: how many convictions within twenty-four months can lead to a hearing suspension? Work out your answer before reading on. The answer is seven. The shorter window is four convictions within twelve months. Either pattern can bring a hearing, and exam or probation failures can too. If the suspension happens, getting the license back costs one hundred dollars, while a revocation costs one hundred twenty-five dollars. Remember that some acts, such as racing or evading arrest, skip the hearing entirely and suspend a license automatically.

lines.text: Patterns: four in twelve, seven in twenty-four.

narration.text: To wrap up, reinstatement costs one hundred dollars, or one hundred twenty-five after a revocation. Some acts, such as racing, evading arrest, or failing to give aid, suspend a license automatically. A hearing can follow four convictions in twelve months or seven in twenty-four. Drivers under twenty-one are suspended automatically for alcohol and drug offenses. Intoxication revocation strikes adults at point zero eight, any refusal, and any detectable alcohol under twenty-one. Courts can compel action for child support and other listed reasons. Next we look at denial, Zero Tolerance, and occupational licenses.

why_how.text: Zero Tolerance protects young drivers by treating any alcohol contact by a minor as an offense.
An occupational license lets a driver with a proven essential need keep driving for that need.

scenario.text: Riley, eighteen, is caught with alcohol for the first time.

reasoning.text: A first Zero Tolerance offense brings a fine up to five hundred dollars, eight to twelve service hours, a course, and a thirty-day suspension.

result.text: Riley pays the fine, completes the hours and the course, and does not drive for thirty days.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing Zero Tolerance applies only when a minor drives after drinking.

correction.text: Zero Tolerance bans all minor alcohol contact, not just drinking and driving.

prompt.text: A teen is caught with alcohol a second time. How long is the suspension?

rationale.text: Zero Tolerance suspensions climb from thirty days on a first offense to sixty on a second and one hundred eighty on a third.

narration.text: This lesson finishes the licensing section with denials and alcohol rules for minors. You will learn the grounds on which a license is denied, how driving while invalid is punished, how Zero Tolerance works for anyone under twenty-one, the penalty for giving alcohol to a minor, and the occupational license a court can grant to someone with an essential need. These rules carry some of the heaviest penalties in the handbook, so they are worth knowing well, and the steps for repeat offenses are a favorite topic for practice questions.

lines.text: Denial for unsafe conditions or debts.

narration.text: A license can be denied for a live disqualification, an unsafe condition, theft, mischief, supplying alcohol to minors, unpaid child support, unpaid fees, missed court, or drugs. Driving while your license is invalid brings penalties that scale up, from a Class C fine through Class B jail to Class A jail with extensions. Skipping traffic court can also block your renewal. Supplying alcohol to a minor risks a fine of up to four thousand dollars, a year in jail, or both. That penalty falls on the adult or friend who supplies the alcohol, not on the minor who receives it.

lines.text: Any minor alcohol contact is banned.
First: up to five hundred dollars.

narration.text: Zero Tolerance bans all alcohol contact for minors. A first offense brings a fine up to five hundred dollars, eight to twelve hours of community service, an alcohol awareness course, and a thirty-day suspension. A second offense brings twenty to forty service hours and a sixty-day suspension. A third offense for someone seventeen to twenty reaches Class B and a one hundred eighty day suspension, with no deferred disposition. For someone under seventeen, a third offense brings sixty days or juvenile court. The penalties climb quickly, so even one offense is costly.

Here is a trap that mixes up two people. When alcohol reaches a minor, two different penalties can apply. The minor faces Zero Tolerance: fines, service hours, a course, and a suspension that climbs with each offense. The person who supplied the alcohol faces a separate penalty, up to four thousand dollars, a year in jail, or both. A practice question might describe an older friend buying drinks for a teen. Ask who the question is about. If it is the teen, think Zero Tolerance. If it is the friend, think of the supplier penalty.

Here is a quick check: a teen is caught with alcohol for the second time under Zero Tolerance. How long is the license suspension? Work out your answer before reading on. It is sixty days. The steps go thirty days for a first offense, sixty for a second, and one hundred eighty for a third when the teen is seventeen to twenty. A second offense also brings twenty to forty hours of community service. The adult who supplied the alcohol would face a separate penalty of up to four thousand dollars, a year in jail, or both.

Let us sum up. A license can be denied for unsafe conditions, theft, unpaid support or fees, missed court, and other grounds, and driving while invalid brings penalties that scale up to jail. Zero Tolerance bans all minor alcohol contact, with suspensions of thirty, sixty, then one hundred eighty days. Supplying alcohol to a minor risks four thousand dollars, a year in jail, or both. A court can grant an occupational license for a proven essential need, at ten dollars yearly or twenty for two, but never for commercial vehicles. That completes the licensing section.
